title: De la Démonomanie des Sorciers
author: Jean Bodin
modern_edition: Bodin, Jean, On the Demon-Mania of Witches, trans. Randy Scott (Victoria: CRRS, 1995)
significance: Written by the era's leading political theorist, this text carried exceptional intellectual authority; its argument that witchcraft posed such extreme danger that normal legal protections should be suspended directly shaped prosecution procedure across France and beyond.
summary: The Démonomanie, in four books, constitutes a comprehensive demonological system by the author of the République. Book I covers the reality of demons and their relations with humans. Book II addresses sorcery and diabolical practices including the sabbath, pact, and maleficium. Book III treats the prosecution of witches, explicitly arguing for suspension of normal evidentiary standards, prohibition of appeal, and use of torture. Book IV attacks skeptics, particularly Johann Weyer, with personal venom. Bodin draws on personal experience as a judge in witchcraft cases and argues from both theological and practical perspectives. His political authority lent the text exceptional credibility.
clark_analysis: Clark emphasizes Bodin's Démonomanie as a prime example of how witch-belief was intellectually serious rather than merely credulous. Bodin was the leading political theorist of the age; his engagement with demonology demonstrates that belief in witchcraft was not confined to the uneducated but was integrated into the highest levels of Renaissance thought.
hutton_analysis: Hutton notes the Démonomanie's practical influence on prosecution procedure and its argument for suspending normal legal protections, which Hutton links to the cascade panics that judicial torture enabled. The text exemplifies how learned demonological authority could translate directly into harsher judicial practice.
ginzburg_analysis: Ginzburg sees Bodin's savage attack on Weyer as revealing the stakes of the skeptical debate: Bodin understood that Weyer's medical defense of accused women threatened the entire juridical-theological system of witch prosecution. The personal venom reflects the depth of the threat Weyer posed.
key_arguments: Witchcraft is real, organized, and poses an extreme threat to Christian society
Normal legal protections must be suspended in witchcraft cases given the gravity and difficulty of proof
Torture is justified and should be used freely to obtain confessions and accomplice names
Weyer's medical defense of accused witches is itself diabolically inspired and dangerous
Judges who release accused witches are as guilty as witches themselves
influence_on_prosecutions: Bodin's argument for suspending normal evidentiary standards was widely cited by prosecutors across France and influenced judicial practice in witch cases throughout the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. His political authority gave these procedural arguments exceptional weight.
scholarly_disagreement: Historians debate whether Bodin's experience as a witch judge preceded or followed the Démonomanie, and how directly his judicial career shaped his arguments. The relationship between his political theory (sovereignty, state power) and his demonology has been analyzed differently by different scholars — some see the witch persecution as an extension of his theory of absolute sovereignty, others treat them as relatively independent.
